content.content:
1	Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.
2	
3	A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.
4	
5	Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.
6	
7	What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself restored to a single, continuous element by the act of closing the clamp, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.
8

1	The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition and with which the axis of a clamped pipe substantially coincides, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.
6	
7	Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
8	
9	The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring 20 nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.
10	
11	The segmented cam ring
12	
13	FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.
14	
15	The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. 17	Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken automatically with each use and requires no separate assembly step.

Each oblique slot 34 passes through the segmented cam ring 20 and is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that circumferential movement of the ring produces a radial displacement of anything constrained to follow the slot. The three oblique slots 34 have the same inclination, so that a given rotation of the coupled ring advances each jaw carriage 30 by the same radial increment. 23	The jaw carriages
24	
25	FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and retains it against radial and axial displacement while permitting it to move circumferentially. The annular guide 18 is formed in both frame halves, one arcuate portion of the annular guide 18 in each frame half, and the two arcuate portions register with one another in the closed condition to form a continuous annular path in which the coupled ring turns.

27	The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. 53	Variations
54

57	Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

input.summary:
Source-fidelity preflight v7 (substantive ledger) on p9, "Self-Centering Split Pipe Clamp With Synchronized Radial Jaws". The inventor authority is a single USER passage in input/conversation.md, identical in substance to input/disclosure.md; there are no corrective or supplemental USER turns. Formalities check out against input/brief.md: title matches the working title exactly, cross-reference and government-support sections both read "Not applicable." (no priority claim, no federally sponsored research), no means-plus-function language appears in the claims, and the abstract runs ~144 words. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions, instructions, unresolved alternatives, or internal comments remain in any file. The numeral table is internally consistent: all 25 numerals are used in the description, every numeral in a figure brief appears in the table, and no numeral carries two meanings (gaps at 42/46/48/60/80 are harmless).

The core of the application traces cleanly: the two semicircular frame halves, hinge and releasable latch, three radial jaw carriages in radial guides, pivoting concave jaw pads with no diameter-specific insert, the segmented cam ring in the annular guide with one segment per half, the complementary coupling faces at hinge and latch ends that couple on closing, followers in oblique slots, the wedge driven by the latch against a ring drive face, the limited stroke, the outward-biasing carriage springs, the two latch positions including the over-center position, the force-limiting spring stack between handle and wedge, the indicator pin moving relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing over a predetermined compression range, the install/remove method, and the optional mounting boss outside the annular guide that takes no part in synchronization. Independent claims 1, 14, and 17 are supported limitation-by-limitation, as are claims 2, 3, 5, 9, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18 and 19.

Fourteen findings follow. Two are critical: an over-center reaction path recited in claim 6 and asserted in the detailed description with no source, and a block of "may be any material / any joint / any complementary shapes / any location" broadening sentences in the Variations paragraph that exist to justify renderer choices. The rest are added structural detail, added performance results, added drive-train members in the FIG. 4 brief, two cross-figure inconsistencies (indicator-pin reference frame, latch-handle attitude, annular-guide lip), and one claim-formality nit. Per scope, prior-art characterizations in the Background were not traced to the disclosure, and no rendered image was inspected.

findings.title: Over-center reaction path holding the latch closed is not disclosed
findings.where: draft/09-claims.md claim 6; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶39 ("The latch and the force-limiting drive train")
findings.detail: Claim 6 recites a specific force path — a reaction travelling from the wedge back to the latch and holding it in the second position — and the description adds both that path (through the force-limiting spring stack) and a "point of maximum resistance". The inventor names an over-center position but never describes any reaction, its route, or a self-holding effect. Common engineering knowledge about over-center linkages is not inventor support, and no USER passage supplies this mechanism.
findings.evidence: Candidate, claim 6: "wherein in the second position a reaction transmitted from the wedge to the latch acts to hold the latch in the second position." Candidate, ¶39: "the latch handle 50 has been carried past the point of maximum resistance, and the reaction transmitted back from the wedge 52 through the force-limiting spring stack 54 acts to hold the latch handle 50 in the second position rather than to open it." Nearest source (conversation.md, USER, ¶11 / disclosure.md ¶9), which shows the gap: "The latch has a first position that holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe." No affirmative passage anywhere describes a reaction, its path, or a holding effect.
findings.fix: Cancel claim 6 and renumber: claims 7–13 become 6–12, claim 14 becomes 13, claims 15–16 become 14–15 (dependency updated to "claim 13"), claim 17 becomes 16, claim 18 becomes 17 (dependency "claim 16"), claims 19–20 become 18–19 (dependency "claim 17"). In ¶39, replace "In a second, over-center position, the latch handle 50 has been carried past the point of maximum resistance, and the reaction transmitted back from the wedge 52 through the force-limiting spring stack 54 acts to hold the latch handle 50 in the second position rather than to open it." with "In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped."

findings.title: Variations paragraph adds unsupported materials, hinge, face-shape and spring-location embodiments
findings.detail: Four of the five sentences in the Variations paragraph broaden the embodiment along axes the inventor never addressed: materials of the frame halves, cam ring, carriages and latch; the hinge as "any joint" swinging "about a fixed axis" and additionally holding the coupling faces in register; the coupling faces as "any complementary shapes"; and the carriage return spring acting "at any location". The third and fifth are the classic pattern of broadening the text to justify a renderer's choice — the plain circumferential faces drawn in the FIG. 2 brief and the flange/ledge spring seat drawn in the FIG. 3 brief. The disclosure says nothing about material, hinge type, hinge axis, face shape, or spring location.
findings.evidence: Candidate, ¶55: "The frame halves, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriages 30, and the latch 16 may be made of any materials having the strength and stiffness required for the loads to be carried. The hinge 14 may be any joint that allows the frame halves to swing apart about a fixed axis at the hinge end while holding the complementary coupling faces 26 in register when the halves are closed. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 may take any complementary shapes that transmit circumferential force between the segments... The carriage return spring 44 of each jaw carriage 30 may act at any location on the jaw carriage 30..." Nearest source (USER): "joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end"; "complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring"; "A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released." The disclosure contains no sentence about materials, hinge construction, face shape, or spring location.
findings.fix: Delete sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 of ¶55, leaving only "The force-limiting spring stack 54 lies in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52." Retain ¶57 unchanged. Do not substitute any replacement generic-shape or optional-material language.

findings.title: "Same inclination" and "equal radial increments" are drafter-supplied slot geometry
findings.detail: The inventor discloses that the oblique slots produce "synchronized inward travel", but never states that the three slots share one inclination or that a given rotation yields equal radial increments. Claim 8 turns that unstated geometry into a claim limitation, and ¶19 and ¶29 assert it as fact about the embodiment.
findings.evidence: Candidate, claim 8: "wherein the three oblique slots have the same inclination such that rotation of the coupled ring through a given angle advances the three jaw carriages by equal radial increments." Candidate, ¶19: "The three oblique slots 34 have the same inclination, so that a given rotation of the coupled ring advances each jaw carriage 30 by the same radial increment." Candidate, ¶29: "Because all three followers 32 are engaged in slots of the same inclination in one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism, by equal radial increments..." Nearest source (USER): "The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages." No passage specifies slot inclination, equality of inclination, or equality of increments.
findings.fix: Cancel claim 8 and renumber accordingly. In ¶19 replace the quoted sentence with "Each oblique slot 34 is inclined so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism." In ¶29 replace "Because all three followers 32 are engaged in slots of the same inclination in one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism, by equal radial increments, for as long as the ring turns." with "Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns." In the FIG. 2 brief, delete "All three are inclined alike."

findings.title: Return rotation of the coupled ring driven by the carriage springs is not disclosed
findings.detail: The candidate recites a reverse drive path in which the carriage return springs push the carriages outward, the followers bear on the opposite sides of the oblique slots, and the coupled ring is turned back through its stroke so that all three pads lift together. The inventor states only that the carriage springs retract the jaws when the latch is released. The reverse force path, the contact on the opposite slot sides, the return rotation of the ring, and the "together" synchronism of retraction are all drafter additions, and one of them is a claim limitation.
findings.evidence: Candidate, claim 7: "wherein the followers and the oblique slots transmit outward movement of the jaw carriages under the carriage return springs into return rotation of the coupled ring when the latch is released, whereby the three jaw pads retract from a pipe received in the frame together." Candidate, ¶33: "the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward, the followers 32 bear on the opposite sides of their oblique slots 34, and the coupled ring is turned back through its stroke." Candidate, claim 20: "so that the followers turn the coupled ring back through the stroke and the three jaw pads lift from the pipe together". Nearest source (USER): "A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released" and "releasing the latch unloads the spring stack and the carriage springs retract the jaws before the frame halves are opened." No passage describes return rotation of the ring or the slot sides that carry it.
findings.fix: Cancel claim 7 and renumber accordingly. In claim 20 replace "retracting the three jaw carriages outwardly under carriage return springs so that the followers turn the coupled ring back through the stroke and the three jaw pads lift from the pipe together" with "retracting the three jaw carriages outwardly under carriage return springs so that the three jaw pads lift from the pipe". In ¶33 replace "the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward, the followers 32 bear on the opposite sides of their oblique slots 34, and the coupled ring is turned back through its stroke. The jaws are thus retracted from the pipe by the same synchronized path, and the clamp 100 is left..." with "the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left...". In ¶51 replace "The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, turning the coupled ring back through its stroke by way of the followers 32 in the oblique slots 34, so that all three jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90 together." with "The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90."

findings.title: Indicator independence from carriage position and the equal-reading result are untraced
findings.detail: The inventor says the indicator reports clamp loading and does not measure pipe diameter. The candidate goes two steps further: claim 4 adds independence from the position of the jaw carriages in the radial guides, and ¶43 asserts a performance result — that a large pipe and a small pipe produce the same predetermined compression range whenever the same clamping force is reached. Neither the carriage-position independence nor the equal-reading result appears in any USER passage.
findings.evidence: Candidate, claim 4: "wherein the indicator pin is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack independently of a diameter of the pipe received in the frame and independently of the position of the jaw carriages in the radial guides." Candidate, ¶43: "It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90 and is not derived from the position of the jaw carriages 30: a large pipe and a small pipe seat the jaw pads 40 at different points in the stroke of the coupled ring, but the indicator pin 56 shows the same predetermined compression range in each case when the same clamping force has been reached." Nearest source (USER): "The indicator reports clamp loading mechanically and does not measure pipe diameter."
findings.fix: Amend claim 4 to end after the disclosed limitation: "wherein the indicator pin is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack independently of a diameter of the pipe received in the frame." In ¶43 replace the quoted sentence with "It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90."

findings.title: FIG. 4 mounts the indicator pin on the handle-side spring seat, contradicting the diameter-independence text
findings.where: figures/fig-04.md ("A slender pin rises from the flat plate...") against draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶43 and draft/09-claims.md claim 4
findings.detail: In the FIG. 4 brief the indicator pin rises from the flat plate that forms the handle-side seat of the force-limiting spring stack, and it is read against the fixed top wall of the latch housing. The plate's position relative to that fixed wall is the sum of the wedge's advance and the stack's compression, and the wedge's advance varies with pipe diameter because the pads seat at different points in the stroke. As depicted, therefore, the pin cannot read stack compression alone, which is exactly what ¶43 and claim 4 assert it does. The depicted arrangement is consistent with the inventor's own statement that the pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the housing; the contradiction is created by the added elaboration, so the text is what should give way.
findings.evidence: Figure brief, FIG. 4: "Above that block, a compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line running from the upper face of the wedge 52 up to a flat plate lying across the cavity. That spring is the force-limiting spring stack 54." ... "A slender pin rises from the flat plate, passes through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58 and stands above it. That pin is the indicator pin 56." Candidate text in conflict, ¶43: "a large pipe and a small pipe seat the jaw pads 40 at different points in the stroke of the coupled ring, but the indicator pin 56 shows the same predetermined compression range in each case". Source (USER) states only: "A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range."
findings.fix: Adopt the fix in the preceding finding — delete the ¶43 elaboration and the tail of claim 4 — and leave the FIG. 4 brief as drawn, since the plate-mounted pin read against a fixed housing edge is the disclosed arrangement. Make no change to the figure brief.

findings.title: Axial retention of the cam ring and "registering" arcuate guide portions are not disclosed
findings.detail: The inventor says only that the segmented cam ring is "retained in an annular guide of the frame" and that one segment is carried by each half. The candidate specifies retention "against radial and axial displacement", adds a retaining lip in the FIG. 3 brief to accomplish the axial part, and recites in claim 10 that the two arcuate guide portions "register with one another in the closed condition". Direction-specific retention and the registration relationship are structural substance with no source passage.
findings.evidence: Candidate, ¶25: "the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and retains it against radial and axial displacement while permitting it to move circumferentially." Candidate, claim 10: "the two arcuate portions registering with one another in the closed condition, each arcuate portion retaining the respective cam ring segment against radial displacement while permitting circumferential movement of that cam ring segment." Figure brief, FIG. 3: "A lip projects downward from the upper wall at the mouth of the groove and reaches part way across it, leaving the rest of the mouth open." ... "A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below and held in by the lip." Nearest source (USER): "A segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half."
findings.fix: In ¶25 replace "retains it against radial and axial displacement while permitting it to move circumferentially" with "retains it while permitting it to move circumferentially". In claim 10 replace "the two arcuate portions registering with one another in the closed condition, each arcuate portion retaining the respective cam ring segment against radial displacement while permitting circumferential movement of that cam ring segment" with "each arcuate portion receiving and retaining the respective cam ring segment while permitting circumferential movement of that cam ring segment". In the FIG. 3 brief delete "A lip projects downward from the upper wall at the mouth of the groove and reaches part way across it, leaving the rest of the mouth open." and amend the following sentence to "...filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below."

findings.title: Spring-stack composition, compliance ranking and force-determination statements are untraced
findings.detail: The disclosure gives one function for the spring stack: additional handle travel after all pads contact the pipe compresses the stack instead of forcing one jaw farther. The candidate adds that the stack is the most compliant element of the drive train once the pads are seated, that the clamping force is determined by stack compression rather than by operator effort, that the stack "comprises one or more resilient elements", and that its combined rate and travel are selected against a load requirement and an "intended range of pipe diameters". None of this composition, ranking, or design criterion appears in any USER passage. "One or more resilient elements arranged in a stack" is also self-inconsistent for the single-element case.
findings.evidence: Candidate, ¶41: "Here the force-limiting spring stack 54 is the most compliant element of the drive train once the jaw pads 40 are seated." ... "the clamping force delivered at the jaw pads 40 is accordingly determined by the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than by how hard the operator pulls the latch handle 50. The force-limiting spring stack 54 comprises one or more resilient elements arranged in a stack whose combined rate and travel are chosen so that the stack is stiff enough to carry the load required to advance the jaw carriages 30 to the pipe 90, and yielding enough to absorb the remaining travel of the latch handle 50 over the intended range of pipe diameters." Nearest source (USER): "A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so additional handle travel after all jaw pads contact the pipe compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others."
findings.fix: Delete from ¶41 the sentence "Here the force-limiting spring stack 54 is the most compliant element of the drive train once the jaw pads 40 are seated."; delete the clause "and the clamping force delivered at the jaw pads 40 is accordingly determined by the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than by how hard the operator pulls the latch handle 50" so the sentence ends at "...farther inward than the others."; and delete the final sentence beginning "The force-limiting spring stack 54 comprises one or more resilient elements..." in its entirety.

findings.title: FIG. 4 brief adds an intermediate link and unrecited latch-housing mountings to the drive train
findings.detail: The FIG. 4 brief inserts a "short link" between the latch handle and the spring seat plate, making the disclosed handle-to-stack path a four-member train. The disclosure places the stack directly between the latch handle and the wedge and names no intermediate member. The plate itself is defensible as a schematic spring seat, but the link is added mechanism, and neither it nor the plate carries a numeral. ¶37 likewise adds that the handle is pivotally mounted on the housing and the wedge is movable in the housing; those assembly relations are minimal but also unstated.
findings.evidence: Figure brief, FIG. 4: "A short link joins the lever to the flat plate, so the lever presses the plate downward." Candidate, ¶37: "a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52." Nearest source (USER): "A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge..." and "A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing...". No passage recites a link, a plate, a handle pivot, or a wedge guide.
findings.fix: In the FIG. 4 brief replace "A short link joins the lever to the flat plate, so the lever presses the plate downward." with "The lever bears directly on the flat plate and presses it downward." and add to the View section: "The flat plate is a spring seat shown schematically." Leave ¶37 as drafted.

findings.title: FIG. 3 flange-and-ledge spring seating is a structural choice not marked as schematic
findings.detail: The brief specifies where the carriage return spring reacts — a ledge projecting from the left wall of the radial guide and a flange on the left side of the jaw carriage. Some pair of seats is unavoidable to depict a compression spring that urges the carriage outward, so this is close to a necessary depiction choice, but as written the brief states a definite connection and location that the disclosure does not give. Marking it schematic keeps the choice confined to the figure brief; note that the corresponding justification sentence in ¶55 ("may act at any location") is separately flagged for deletion.
findings.evidence: Figure brief, FIG. 3: "a ledge projects into it from its left wall near the lower end" and "A flange on the left side of the jaw carriage 30 stands above the ledge, and a compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line from the underside of the flange down to the ledge. That spring is the carriage return spring 44." Nearest source (USER): "A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released."
findings.fix: Add to the FIG. 3 View section: "The ledge, the flange and the spring between them are shown schematically." Make no corresponding addition to the description or claims.

findings.title: Annular guide 18 is drawn with a retaining lip in FIG. 3 and without one in FIG. 5
findings.detail: Both briefs section the same annular guide 18 in a plane containing a radial direction and the frame axis, and both describe a groove wider than deep, closed at the right and opening toward the left. FIG. 3 adds a lip at the mouth that holds the cam ring in; FIG. 5 has no such feature. The same numbered part is therefore given two different cross-sections.
findings.evidence: FIG. 3: "A lip projects downward from the upper wall at the mouth of the groove and reaches part way across it... A hatched block lies in the groove... held in by the lip." FIG. 5: "A groove is formed in it, wider than it is deep, bounded by the body on its radially outer side above and its radially inner side below, closed at its right and opening toward the left of the view. That groove is the annular guide 18. A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it in the radial direction with a small running clearance at the walls above and below."
findings.fix: Resolve in favour of FIG. 5 by deleting the lip from the FIG. 3 brief as set out in the axial-retention finding above, so both figures show the same groove profile.

findings.title: Latch handle attitude differs between FIG. 1 and FIG. 4
findings.detail: Both figures show the clamp in the same state — FIG. 1 is the closed condition with the jaw pads on the pipe, which is the clamped, over-center state depicted in FIG. 4 — and FIG. 4 is expressly "viewed as in FIG. 1" with radially outward toward the top. In FIG. 4 the handle rises from the housing and leans circumferentially away from the ring, passing out above the housing's right wall. In FIG. 1 it lies alongside the outer boundary of the second frame half, i.e. tangentially against the ring. A reader comparing the two sheets sees the same lever in two different attitudes.
findings.evidence: FIG. 1: "At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block lying outside the outer boundary of the ring and bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending from the block alongside the outer boundary of the second frame half 12." FIG. 4: "An elongated lever is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle in the upper right of the cavity and extends upward and to the right, passing out above the right wall... The lever leans right, past the upright, in the over-centre position."
findings.fix: In the FIG. 1 brief replace "with an elongated lever extending from the block alongside the outer boundary of the second frame half 12" with "with an elongated lever extending from the block outward and away from the ring, on the side of the block remote from the second frame half 12, so that it stands as it does in FIG. 4".

Both are plausible consequences of disclosed structure, but neither is stated in any USER passage, and result statements of this kind are read against the claims.
findings.evidence: Candidate, ¶17: "so that the coupling is made and broken automatically with each use and requires no separate assembly step." data.summary:
Source-fidelity preflight v7 (substantive ledger) on p9, "Self-Centering Split Pipe Clamp With Synchronized Radial Jaws". The inventor authority is a single USER passage in input/conversation.md, identical in substance to input/disclosure.md; there are no corrective or supplemental USER turns. Formalities check out against input/brief.md: title matches the working title exactly, cross-reference and government-support sections both read "Not applicable." (no priority claim, no federally sponsored research), no means-plus-function language appears in the claims, and the abstract runs ~144 words. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions, instructions, unresolved alternatives, or internal comments remain in any file. The numeral table is internally consistent: all 25 numerals are used in the description, every numeral in a figure brief appears in the table, and no numeral carries two meanings (gaps at 42/46/48/60/80 are harmless).

The core of the application traces cleanly: the two semicircular frame halves, hinge and releasable latch, three radial jaw carriages in radial guides, pivoting concave jaw pads with no diameter-specific insert, the segmented cam ring in the annular guide with one segment per half, the complementary coupling faces at hinge and latch ends that couple on closing, followers in oblique slots, the wedge driven by the latch against a ring drive face, the limited stroke, the outward-biasing carriage springs, the two latch positions including the over-center position, the force-limiting spring stack between handle and wedge, the indicator pin moving relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing over a predetermined compression range, the install/remove method, and the optional mounting boss outside the annular guide that takes no part in synchronization. Independent claims 1, 14, and 17 are supported limitation-by-limitation, as are claims 2, 3, 5, 9, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18 and 19.

Fourteen findings follow. Two are critical: an over-center reaction path recited in claim 6 and asserted in the detailed description with no source, and a block of "may be any material / any joint / any complementary shapes / any location" broadening sentences in the Variations paragraph that exist to justify renderer choices. The rest are added structural detail, added performance results, added drive-train members in the FIG. 4 brief, two cross-figure inconsistencies (indicator-pin reference frame, latch-handle attitude, annular-guide lip), and one claim-formality nit. Per scope, prior-art characterizations in the Background were not traced to the disclosure, and no rendered image was inspected.

findings.title: Over-center reaction path holding the latch closed is not disclosed
findings.where: draft/09-claims.md claim 6; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶39 ("The latch and the force-limiting drive train")
findings.detail: Claim 6 recites a specific force path — a reaction travelling from the wedge back to the latch and holding it in the second position — and the description adds both that path (through the force-limiting spring stack) and a "point of maximum resistance". The inventor names an over-center position but never describes any reaction, its route, or a self-holding effect. Common engineering knowledge about over-center linkages is not inventor support, and no USER passage supplies this mechanism.
findings.evidence: Candidate, claim 6: "wherein in the second position a reaction transmitted from the wedge to the latch acts to hold the latch in the second position." Candidate, ¶39: "the latch handle 50 has been carried past the point of maximum resistance, and the reaction transmitted back from the wedge 52 through the force-limiting spring stack 54 acts to hold the latch handle 50 in the second position rather than to open it." Nearest source (conversation.md, USER, ¶11 / disclosure.md ¶9), which shows the gap: "The latch has a first position that holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe." No affirmative passage anywhere describes a reaction, its path, or a holding effect.
findings.fix: Cancel claim 6 and renumber: claims 7–13 become 6–12, claim 14 becomes 13, claims 15–16 become 14–15 (dependency updated to "claim 13"), claim 17 becomes 16, claim 18 becomes 17 (dependency "claim 16"), claims 19–20 become 18–19 (dependency "claim 17"). In ¶39, replace "In a second, over-center position, the latch handle 50 has been carried past the point of maximum resistance, and the reaction transmitted back from the wedge 52 through the force-limiting spring stack 54 acts to hold the latch handle 50 in the second position rather than to open it." with "In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped."

findings.title: Variations paragraph adds unsupported materials, hinge, face-shape and spring-location embodiments
findings.detail: Four of the five sentences in the Variations paragraph broaden the embodiment along axes the inventor never addressed: materials of the frame halves, cam ring, carriages and latch; the hinge as "any joint" swinging "about a fixed axis" and additionally holding the coupling faces in register; the coupling faces as "any complementary shapes"; and the carriage return spring acting "at any location". The third and fifth are the classic pattern of broadening the text to justify a renderer's choice — the plain circumferential faces drawn in the FIG. 2 brief and the flange/ledge spring seat drawn in the FIG. 3 brief. The disclosure says nothing about material, hinge type, hinge axis, face shape, or spring location.
findings.evidence: Candidate, ¶55: "The frame halves, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriages 30, and the latch 16 may be made of any materials having the strength and stiffness required for the loads to be carried. The hinge 14 may be any joint that allows the frame halves to swing apart about a fixed axis at the hinge end while holding the complementary coupling faces 26 in register when the halves are closed. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 may take any complementary shapes that transmit circumferential force between the segments... The carriage return spring 44 of each jaw carriage 30 may act at any location on the jaw carriage 30..." Nearest source (USER): "joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end"; "complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring"; "A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released." The disclosure contains no sentence about materials, hinge construction, face shape, or spring location.
findings.fix: Delete sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 of ¶55, leaving only "The force-limiting spring stack 54 lies in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52." Retain ¶57 unchanged. Do not substitute any replacement generic-shape or optional-material language.

findings.title: "Same inclination" and "equal radial increments" are drafter-supplied slot geometry
findings.detail: The inventor discloses that the oblique slots produce "synchronized inward travel", but never states that the three slots share one inclination or that a given rotation yields equal radial increments. Claim 8 turns that unstated geometry into a claim limitation, and ¶19 and ¶29 assert it as fact about the embodiment.
findings.evidence: Candidate, claim 8: "wherein the three oblique slots have the same inclination such that rotation of the coupled ring through a given angle advances the three jaw carriages by equal radial increments." Candidate, ¶19: "The three oblique slots 34 have the same inclination, so that a given rotation of the coupled ring advances each jaw carriage 30 by the same radial increment." Candidate, ¶29: "Because all three followers 32 are engaged in slots of the same inclination in one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism, by equal radial increments..." Nearest source (USER): "The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages." No passage specifies slot inclination, equality of inclination, or equality of increments.
findings.fix: Cancel claim 8 and renumber accordingly. In ¶19 replace the quoted sentence with "Each oblique slot 34 is inclined so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism." In ¶29 replace "Because all three followers 32 are engaged in slots of the same inclination in one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism, by equal radial increments, for as long as the ring turns." with "Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns." findings.detail: The candidate recites a reverse drive path in which the carriage return springs push the carriages outward, the followers bear on the opposite sides of the oblique slots, and the coupled ring is turned back through its stroke so that all three pads lift together. The inventor states only that the carriage springs retract the jaws when the latch is released. findings.title: FIG. 4 mounts the indicator pin on the handle-side spring seat, contradicting the diameter-independence text
findings.where: figures/fig-04.md ("A slender pin rises from the flat plate...") against draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶43 and draft/09-claims.md claim 4
findings.detail: In the FIG. 4 brief the indicator pin rises from the flat plate that forms the handle-side seat of the force-limiting spring stack, and it is read against the fixed top wall of the latch housing. The plate's position relative to that fixed wall is the sum of the wedge's advance and the stack's compression, and the wedge's advance varies with pipe diameter because the pads seat at different points in the stroke. As depicted, therefore, the pin cannot read stack compression alone, which is exactly what ¶43 and claim 4 assert it does. The depicted arrangement is consistent with the inventor's own statement that the pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the housing; the contradiction is created by the added elaboration, so the text is what should give way.
findings.evidence: Figure brief, FIG. 4: "Above that block, a compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line running from the upper face of the wedge 52 up to a flat plate lying across the cavity. That spring is the force-limiting spring stack 54." ... "A slender pin rises from the flat plate, passes through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58 and stands above it. That pin is the indicator pin 56." Candidate text in conflict, ¶43: "a large pipe and a small pipe seat the jaw pads 40 at different points in the stroke of the coupled ring, but the indicator pin 56 shows the same predetermined compression range in each case". findings.fix: Adopt the fix in the preceding finding — delete the ¶43 elaboration and the tail of claim 4 — and leave the FIG. 4 brief as drawn, since the plate-mounted pin read against a fixed housing edge is the disclosed arrangement. Make no change to the figure brief.
